item.research_question: Can high-entropy transition-metal carbides be designed to exhibit tunable plasmonic properties in the near-IR to visible range while maintaining high thermal stability and mechanical hardness?
item.material_system: High-entropy transition-metal carbides (PHECs), specifically the archetype HfTa4C5 and a set of 14 six-element alloys (Carbon + 5 transition metals from groups 4, 5, and 6: Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, W)
item.processing_route: Computational: High-throughput disorder modeling using the Partial Occupation (POCC) method within the AFLOW framework to generate Boltzmann ensembles of superlattices, followed by time-dependent density-functional perturbation theory (TD-DFPT) calculations using VASP and turboEELS. Experimental: Ball-milling of TaC and HfC powders (4:1 ratio) followed by Field Assisted Sintering Technology (FAST) at 2100–2400 °C, 40–55 MPa, and 30–40 min hold times.
item.test_conditions: Computational: Optical limit (q=0) and varying transferred momentum (q); temperatures up to 1500 K. Experimental: Electron-energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) on HfTa4C5 cross-sections at beam energy 300 keV, with temperatures ranging from room temperature (~25 °C) to 1200 °C.
key_findings: HfTa4C5 exhibits a crossover energy (E0) at 2.41 eV (simulated) and 2.7 eV (experimental), marking a metal-to-dielectric transition in the visible range.
The plasmonic response of PHECs can be tuned from the near-IR to visible by varying the transition metal components and their concentration.
Systems 3-HfNbTaTiZrC5 and 14-HfNbTaTiWC5 show the highest effective EELS intensity (h) and lowest energy loss dissipation, indicating good plasmonic properties.
The crossover energy E0 spans a wide range from near-IR to visible, increasing monotonically with the atomic number of constituents within each group.
The screened plasmon resonance in HfTa4C5 remains clearly recognizable up to 1500 K, demonstrating stability far above the melting points of standard plasmonic metals like Ag and Au.
Substitution of Hf with 3d metals (V, Cr) leads to plasmonic resonance deterioration, while group 6 metals (W, Mo) cause broadening of the EELS peak.
The presence of Ta is necessary but not sufficient for obtaining good plasmonic PHECs; the best results come from combining high-Z elements from groups 4 and 5 (Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta).
item.mechanism: The plasmonic response arises from a balance between intraband transitions (Drude-like, negative contribution to real dielectric function) and interband transitions (positive contribution). The crossover energy E0 corresponds to the energy where the real part of the dielectric function switches sign, determined by the energy difference (δ) between the Fermi level and the edge of the interband transition band (b2). Higher atomic number elements shift the Fermi level deeper into the d-band, increasing δ and causing a blue-shift in E0.
item.limitations: The study does not include time evolution or de-excitation processes of plasmons, which are affected by electron-phonon scattering. Experimental characterization beyond 1500 K is noted as arduous due to equipment limitations. Some systems exhibit high dissipation where peaks cannot be associated with collective plasmon-like oscillations.
item.future_work: The authors propose using the discovered rules to design tailored high-entropy ceramics with optical properties optimized for specific applications, such as exploiting dissipative systems for photothermal applications or using quasi-neutral elements (Ti, W) to stabilize PHECs while altering mechanical/thermal properties.
quotes: We chose high-entropy transition-metal carbides because of their exceptional thermal, chemical stability, and mechanical properties.
E0—so-called crossover energy—identifies the energy at which the real part of the dielectric function switches sign ( − → +, see Fig. 1).
The plasmon resonance is surprisingly stable even at high temperature, much higher than the standard plasmonic metals' melting points (e.g., Ag and Au).
